That filter starts at `reader`, but `PlatformAccount` rows are visible from `partial`. So the `PlatformAccount` select policy reads the definer view `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` instead. Unlike a function, Postgres can inline a view, so one account is checked per row through the primary key, and a full read builds its set once. Three things about this view must stay:

- `DISTINCT`, and no `space_id` column. One row per membership would reveal memberships that `LocalAccess` hides below `reader`.
- `security_barrier`. Without it, a caller's filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` can run below the access join and see accounts from other spaces.
- Its grants: `SELECT` only. `anon` holds it for public access (see [Grants made for public access](#grants-made-for-public-access)). It returns no rows to `anon` today.

### Account and group writes

- `authenticated` can't insert into `PlatformAccount`, and has `UPDATE` on it per column, so clients can't set who owns an account (`dg_account`) or change what identifies it (`agent_type`, `platform`, `account_local_id`). A new column isn't client-writable until it's added to the grant. Clients create and upsert accounts through `upsert_account_in_space`, which also adds the account to the space (ENG-2447).
- `upsert_account_in_space` requires editor access to the space, and grants no `SpaceAccess` (ENG-2439). `LocalAccess` says an account belongs to a space and grants nothing.
- `LocalAccess` writes require editor access to the row's own space (ENG-2447).
- Only a group's admins can add members. The `create-group` edge function adds the first admin with the service role, and `accept_group_invitation` adds invited members (ENG-2438).

### Account reads

- `authenticated` has `SELECT` on `PlatformAccount` per column, without `dg_account` and `metadata`, and `my_accounts` leaves out both columns too (ENG-2441). `dg_account` would show which accounts belong to one person, and nothing uses `metadata` yet.
- A column grant applies to every row, so clients can't read their own `dg_account` from the table either. They get their own user id from their session, and their own accounts from `my_platform_account_ids`.
- Clients must name the columns they read from `PlatformAccount`. `select("*")`, and any filter on a hidden column, fails with a permission error.
- `my_pseudo_accounts` returns `dg_account`, so it has to stay a definer view. Any `anon` grant on `PlatformAccount` has to use the same column list.

### The `my_*` views

The `my_*` views (`my_spaces`, `my_accounts`, `my_concepts`, `my_contents`, `my_documents`, `my_file_references`, `my_contents_with_embedding_openai_text_embedding_3_small_1536`, `my_pseudo_accounts`, `my_groups`) are the main way clients read data.

They are not `security_invoker`: they run as their owner, bypass RLS, and apply their own access filter. This was done for speed, when policies called their helpers once per row and large reads timed out (ENG-1433, ENG-1435). The views compute the user's accessible spaces once per query, in the InitPlan form above (ENG-2344, ENG-2359).

The policies now use that form too, but most views stay definer, because they're still faster. Under RLS, a filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` has to run after the policy, so it can't use an index. `concept_in_relations` filters with `@>`, and took about 250 times as long through RLS with 273 `ResourceAccess` rows. Reading the tables directly has the same cost. So by default, clients read through these views and write to the tables. The timings are on ENG-2444, which is parked.

Consequences:

- Each view's filter is a second copy of the table's access rules. A change to a policy must be repeated in the views that read the table. We accept this cost, and the security advisor keeps reporting these views.
- Single-table views are automatically updatable, and writes through them would also bypass RLS. Clients only read views, so write privileges are revoked from client roles on every view (ENG-2368, ENG-2359, ENG-2466). The default privileges give them back to `authenticated` on a new view, so it needs the same `REVOKE`.
- Clients depend on the view names and columns, including older plugin versions that are still installed, PostgREST's foreign-key inference and the generated types. Keep them stable.
- They have no `security_barrier`, so a caller's filter that isn't `LEAKPROOF` can run below the access filter and see rows the view would hide (measured on `my_accounts`). PostgREST's fixed filter operators shouldn't allow such a filter, so this matters for direct SQL access. The same reordering is what lets `@>` use its index, so time the relation queries before adding `security_barrier` to `my_concepts`.

## Grants and default privileges

`base.sql` sets the default privileges of every object that `postgres` creates in `public`:

| Role            | Tables and views                       | Sequences         | Functions |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------- | --------- |
| `anon`          | nothing                                | nothing           | nothing   |
| `authenticated` | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` | `USAGE`, `SELECT` | `EXECUTE` |
| `service_role`  | everything                             | everything        | `EXECUTE` |

We set these ourselves because the Supabase image's defaults change between versions. Image 17.11.0.018 gives client roles only `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, `TRIGGER` and `MAINTAIN` on new tables, and nothing on new sequences or functions, so a database built on it from migrations that relied on the image was unusable (ENG-2466).

Because `authenticated` can read and write a new table or view from the start:

- A new table must enable RLS. Without it, every signed-in user can read and write every row, in every space.
- A new view must run as the caller (`security_invoker`), or filter by the caller as the `my_*` views do. A definer view without such a filter shows every row to every signed-in user.

`base.sql` also revokes `PUBLIC` from the global function defaults of the `postgres` role. Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to `PUBLIC`, and `anon` inherits it. A schema-level default cannot remove a global one, so this also applies to functions that `postgres` creates in other schemas.

The schema files declare only the exceptions to these defaults, next to the object, with a `--` comment saying which client or policy needs them: every `anon` grant, and every privilege removed from `authenticated` or `service_role`. Functions that are not `SECURITY DEFINER` and don't write run as the caller under RLS, so they are granted to `anon` as a group, at the end of their schema file. Don't write `GRANT ALL ... TO authenticated`: on a table, it includes `TRUNCATE`, which RLS doesn't limit.

`CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` keeps a function's grants, but `DROP FUNCTION` followed by `CREATE FUNCTION` loses them. A migration that recreates a function must repeat its exceptions, such as an `anon` grant. Dropping a view also drops the functions that return its row type, such as `author_of_concept` and `author_of_content` for `my_accounts`, so they need their grants repeated too. `REVOKE ALL ON TABLE` also removes the table's column grants, such as those on `PlatformAccount`.

### Rules

1. A function or view used by a policy must be usable by every role that queries that table: EXECUTE on the function, SELECT on the view. Without it, the query fails with a permission error; it does not return zero rows.
2. Functions called in a view are checked against the role querying the view, not the view owner. A function that is not `SECURITY DEFINER` also runs its body as that role, under the policies of whatever it reads. For example, the views call `my_accessible_resources()`, which reads `ResourceAccess` as the caller.
3. Trigger functions need no grant. Postgres checks EXECUTE when the trigger is created, not when it fires.
4. A `SECURITY DEFINER` function that clients can call must check the caller's access itself, because it skips RLS. Don't rely on capping a permission with `least(...)`: `LEAST` ignores NULL, so a caller with no access (NULL) gets the other argument.
5. A helper that clients can call may reveal only facts about the caller, facts about resources the caller can read, or facts about identities whose owner made them public.

One helper doesn't follow rule 5 yet. `file_exists` says whether any space holds a file with a given hash; the caller must already know the hash.

### Functions `anon` can execute

| Function           | Why                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `get_secret_token` | The website's `/auth/token` route, which hands a plugin's session to a browser that isn't logged in yet. The token is 12 random bytes, single use, with a 45-second expiry for this flow |
| `my_user_accounts` | Public access: base of the views and helpers                                                                                                                                             |
| `my_space_ids`     | `Space` select policy; `anon` can read `Space`. Public access: the `my_*` views and the other select policies                                                                            |
| `file_access`      | Public access: the storage read policy on the `assets` bucket                                                                                                                            |

All other `SECURITY DEFINER` functions, and the functions that write, are executable by `authenticated` only. Trigger functions, and `is_last_local_reference` (which only triggers call), are executable by neither role.

`in_space` is not executable by `anon`. Only write paths reach it as the caller, and `anon`'s reads use `my_space_ids`.

`anon` holds only `SELECT` on the contributor tables, and its reads fail with a permission error on `ResourceAccess` until public access adds the grants below.

### Grants made for public access

`anon` will read public nodes, their files and their authors (ENG-1837). The "Public access" entries above, and `anon`'s `SELECT` on `Space`, the contributor tables and the views, are grants made ahead of that work. `anon` can't execute the functions that write, except `get_secret_token`. Keep them: rule 1 means that removing one fails those queries with a permission error. ENG-1837 also has to grant `anon` `SELECT` on `Concept`, `Content`, `Document`, `FileReference` and `ResourceAccess`, and open `storage_select_assets_access` to `anon`, which today applies only to `authenticated`.

## Supabase advisor findings that remain

Supabase runs two advisors on the database, one for security and one for performance. Both check shapes, not behaviour, so some of their findings are expected and stay.

### Security advisor

It flags any view that bypasses RLS, any view that reads `auth.users`, any policy whose condition is always true, and any `SECURITY DEFINER` function a client role can execute. It can't tell whether a function or view leaks anything. These findings are expected:

- `my_groups` reads `auth.users` (`auth_users_exposed` and `security_definer_view`). Groups are rows in `auth.users`, with the synthetic email `{group name}@groups.discoursegraphs.com` set by the `create-group` edge function. The view returns only the id and name of the groups the current user belongs to; `anon` gets no rows. It must run as its owner, because clients can't read `auth.users`. This stays.
- The other eight `my_*` views (`security_definer_view`). This is the speed workaround described above.
- `accounts_in_my_partial_spaces` (`security_definer_view`). It runs as its owner on purpose, to read `LocalAccess` below `reader` (see above). It stays.
- `anon_security_definer_function_executable` for the four functions in the table above.
- `authenticated_security_definer_function_executable` for the policy helpers and for the functions that clients call directly: `create_account_in_space`, `upsert_accounts_in_space`, `file_exists`, `create_secret_token`, `get_secret_token`, `accept_group_invitation`. Also for `upsert_account_in_space`: no client calls it, but `upsert_content` and `upsert_documents` run as the caller, so the caller needs `EXECUTE`.

### Performance advisor

These findings are expected:

- `FileReference_content_fkey` (`unindexed_foreign_keys`). Deleting a `Content` row looks up its `FileReference` rows through the primary key `(source_local_id, space_id, filepath)`. The advisor flags it only because the key's column order differs from the foreign key's.
- The foreign keys from `AgentIdentifier.account_id`, `LocalAccess.space_id`, `SpaceAccess.space_id`, `concept_contributors.contributor_id` and `content_contributors.contributor_id` (`unindexed_foreign_keys`). Only deleting an account or a space would use an index on them, and both are rare. Revisit if either becomes routine.
- The foreign keys from `Concept.author_id`, `Content.author_id`, `Content.creator_id` and `Document.author_id` (`unindexed_foreign_keys`). An index would help account deletion and queries by author, neither of which is in use yet, and every sync insert would pay for it. Decide when the first feature that needs one is planned, measured against its queries. A composite index such as `(space_id, author_id)` may fit better, since reads are already scoped to a list of spaces.
- `Content_text` (`unused_index`). Kept for database searches on content text, which are planned but not yet used.

Any other finding from either advisor is new, and should be fixed or added here with its reason.

## Checklist for changes

- New table: enable RLS, because `authenticated` can read and write it by default. Write policies for each operation, and grant `anon` only what anonymous readers need. Add visibility scenarios to `features/`, like `features/conceptAccess.feature`.
- New policy: wrap calls that don't depend on the row in `(SELECT ...)`. Write `(SELECT auth.uid())`, not `auth.uid()`. Don't pass a row column to a helper that sets `search_path`. If the policy reads another table directly, remember that table's own select policy filters what it sees.
- New `PlatformAccount` column: decide whether clients may read or write it, and add it to the per-column grants if so.
- New `SECURITY DEFINER` function: set `search_path = ''`, check the caller's access inside it (rule 4), grant it only to the roles that call it, and add a comment saying who that is.
- New function that `anon` reaches, directly, through a policy or through a view: grant it to `anon` in its schema file and in the migration.
- New trigger function: revoke it from `authenticated`.
- New or changed view: keep existing names and columns, and mirror the table's access rules. Revoke `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` from `authenticated`, and grant `SELECT` to `anon` if anonymous readers need it.
- New definer view: filter by the caller, set `security_barrier`, and return only what every caller may already see, including through row counts.
- Before merging, run the cucumber suite and compare both Supabase advisors' lists with the findings above.

## History

- ENG-950, ENG-1433, ENG-1435: the `my_*` views, introduced to avoid per-row policy costs.
- ENG-2344, ENG-2359: the views rewritten with InitPlans.
- ENG-2368: write privileges revoked on the updatable views.
- ENG-1480, ENG-2436: Supabase findings reviewed and documented.
- ENG-2438: joining a group limited to its admins, and `group_exists` removed.
- ENG-2439: `upsert_account_in_space` requires editor access and grants no `SpaceAccess`.
- ENG-2441: `dg_account` and `metadata` removed from `my_accounts` and hidden on `PlatformAccount`.
- ENG-2442: function grants made explicit, and new functions no longer executable by `anon`.
- ENG-2443, ENG-2446: policies moved to the InitPlan form, and `can_access_account`, `can_view_concept`, `can_view_content`, `account_in_shared_space`, `unowned_account_in_shared_space` and `is_my_account` removed.
- ENG-2447: account columns granted individually, and `LocalAccess` writes checked against the row's space.
- ENG-2448: the unused `access_token` table removed.
- ENG-2466: default privileges set in `base.sql` instead of taken from the Supabase image, and every existing object's grants made explicit. Client roles lost `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, `TRIGGER` and `MAINTAIN`, write privileges on the views, and `UPDATE` on sequences. `anon` lost its writes on `Space` and `EXECUTE` on the functions that write. `authenticated` lost `INSERT` on `Space`, since only create-space creates spaces, and `space_insert_policy` was removed.

content.text:
Marc-Antoine didn't answer yes or no. Instead he pointed at his cleanup, and on `origin/main` that cleanup has already done what we asked about. So nothing breaks, and the spec's premise is now out of date.

**What's on main now** (ENG-2442 [#1604](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1604) and ENG-2466 [#1610](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1610)):
- `base.sql` removes `PUBLIC` from the default `EXECUTE` on new functions.
- The `20261106130000_explicit_privileges` migration removes all of `PUBLIC`'s, `anon`'s and `authenticated`'s rights on every existing function, then grants each one again explicitly. `PUBLIC` holds `EXECUTE` on no function now.
- `packages/database/doc/security_model.md` sets the rules, plus a heuristic for deciding new functions:
  - `authenticated` gets `EXECUTE` by default.
  - `anon` gets nothing by default. It's granted a set of read-only functions that run as the caller under RLS, plus four `SECURITY DEFINER` ones. Those grants prepare for public access (ENG-1837), and he wants to keep them.

**What this changes in our spec:**
1. **Decision 4 is wrong on two facts.** It says `PUBLIC` holds `EXECUTE` on every function, and that `base.sql` grants functions to `anon`. Neither is true anymore.
2. **Task 1.2 shrinks.** There's no `PUBLIC` revoke left to do, and no hosted-database check beyond deploying the migrations. All that remains is granting `mcp_reader` an explicit allowlist.
3. **There's a new upkeep cost.** `mcp_reader` isn't covered by the default privileges, so every new read function needs its own grant to it. Rule 1 in his doc also says a function a policy or view calls must be granted to every role that queries it, or the query fails with a permission error. `anon`'s grant list is the obvious template for the allowlist.

He said his permissions are open for discussion, but nothing in our spec needs to change his grants.

**Database access controls**

- **Row-level security.** 61 of the 65 row-level security policies have no `TO` clause, so they apply to every database role. The other four are `TO authenticated` on `storage.objects` (file storage), which retrieval doesn't read. Table grants go only to `authenticated` (the signed-in role) and `service_role`.
- **Function privileges.** `PUBLIC` (every database role) can execute every function in the `public` schema, because no schema file revokes that default. Some write functions are `SECURITY DEFINER` (they run as their owner, not as the caller), such as `create_secret_token` and `accept_group_invitation`. So table grants alone don't stop them.
- **Auth settings.** `config.toml` sets `jwt_expiry = 3600` (a session token lasts one hour). The custom access token hook is commented out.

----
**The hook.** A custom access token hook (a database function Supabase calls on every token issue and refresh) checks the token's `session_id`. When the session is in `mcp_session` (list of handed-over sessions), it sets the token's `role` claim to `mcp_reader` (read-only database role; name proposed). Other sessions keep `authenticated`.

**The role.** `mcp_reader`:

- is granted to `authenticator` (the role Supabase's REST layer logs in as), so requests can switch to it;
- has `SELECT` on the tables and views retrieval reads, and no `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE`;
- has `EXECUTE` only on an allowlist: the search RPC, plus the access helpers that the policies and views call.

**Locking down functions.** `PUBLIC` (every database role) holds `EXECUTE` on every function, so the allowlist needs two changes:

- `REVOKE EXECUTE ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC`;
- the matching default-privilege change, so new functions aren't executable by default either.

**This doesn't change what plugins or sync can do.** `base.sql` runs first and sets default privileges that grant every later function to `anon` and `authenticated` explicitly. So the plugins' roles don't rely on `PUBLIC`, and they keep every function they can call today. Postgres has no deny grant, and every role inherits `PUBLIC`, so removing that default is the only way to keep a function from `mcp_reader`. Before the revoke, a check on the hosted database confirms that `anon` and `authenticated` hold `EXECUTE` on every function. Its migrations predate the schema files, so it could differ.

A test lists every function `mcp_reader` can execute and compares the list with the allowlist. Policies without a `TO` clause cover `mcp_reader`, so its reads follow the space account's current access.

----
- [A switched-off hook fails open] → Handed-over sessions would get `authenticated`, which can write. The MCP's startup role check catches this. A harness that calls Supabase directly would still get a write-capable session.
- [A grant is missing from `mcp_reader`] → Retrieval fails or returns fewer rows. The API integration tests run every operation with a handed-over session, so as `mcp_reader`.
- [Revoking from `PUBLIC` breaks a function that relied on it] → Unlikely, because `base.sql` grants every function to `anon` and `authenticated` explicitly (Decision 4). Check the hosted database's grants before the revoke, and run the full cucumber suite as `anon` and `authenticated` after it.
- [The MCP depends on the website] → If the website is down, MCP retrieval fails with `dependency_error`, and every call takes one extra network hop. Accepted in exchange for one contract and server-side fixes.
- [`/api/v1` is pinned by installed copies] → Change it only additively. A breaking change ships as `/api/v2` alongside `v1`.
---

- [ ] 1.1 Add `mcp_reader` (read-only database role). Grant it to `authenticator` (the role Supabase's REST layer logs in as). Give it `SELECT` on the tables and views retrieval reads. Verify: `pnpm check-schema` passes, and a cucumber scenario shows that `mcp_reader` reads only what the space account can read.
- [ ] 1.2 Revoke `EXECUTE` on `public` functions from `PUBLIC` (every database role), including the default privileges. Then grant `mcp_reader` `EXECUTE` on an allowlist of the access helpers that policies and views call. Verify:
  - a test lists every function `mcp_reader` can execute, and matches it against the allowlist;
  - the full cucumber suite still passes as `anon` and as `authenticated`;
  - before the revoke, a query on the hosted database shows that `anon` and `authenticated` hold `EXECUTE` on every `public` function (`has_function_privilege`).
- [ ] 1.3 Add a custom access token hook (assigns a role at sign-in). When the token's `session_id` is in `mcp_session` (list of handed-over sessions), it sets `role` to `mcp_reader`. Otherwise it returns the claims unchanged. Enable it in `config.toml`, and document how to enable it on the hosted project. Verify: cucumber scenarios for
  - an MCP session getting `mcp_reader`, both on issue and on refresh;

content.text:
Here are the draft edits. Nothing is written yet. They update the spec to match Marc-Antoine's cleanup on `origin/main` (ENG-2442 and ENG-2466).

**1. `design.md`, Context → Database access controls**

Row-level security: the counts changed on main, and `anon` now holds some grants.
> 58 of the 62 row-level security policies have no `TO` clause, so they apply to every database role. The other four are `TO authenticated` on `storage.objects` (file storage), which retrieval doesn't read. Table grants go to `authenticated` (the signed-in role) and `service_role`. `anon` holds `SELECT` on `Space`, the contributor tables and the `my_*` views, ahead of public access ([ENG-1837](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1837)).

Function privileges:
> **Function privileges.** No function is executable through `PUBLIC` (every database role). `base.sql` removes that default, and every function is granted explicitly. `authenticated` gets every new function by default. `anon` gets only a listed set of read-only functions. `packages/database/doc/security_model.md` gives the rules and the heuristic for granting new functions. Some write functions are `SECURITY DEFINER` (they run as their owner, not as the caller), such as `create_secret_token` and `accept_group_invitation`. Each is granted to `authenticated` only.

**2. `design.md`, Decision 4.** Drop the "Locking down functions" paragraph and the "This doesn't change what plugins or sync can do" paragraph, and put this in their place:
> **Granting functions.** No function is executable through `PUBLIC`, and the default privileges don't cover a new role, so `mcp_reader` starts with no `EXECUTE`. It gets an explicit allowlist: the search RPC, plus the functions that the policies and views it reads call. The allowlist starts from `anon`'s read-only set, which public access already uses. A function a policy or view calls must be granted to every role that queries it, or the query fails with a permission error ([security model](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/blob/main/packages/database/doc/security_model.md), rule 1). So a new read function that retrieval reaches needs a grant to `mcp_reader` too. Plugin and sync grants don't change.

The "A test lists every function…" paragraph stays as it is.

**3. `design.md`, Risks.** Replace the "Revoking from `PUBLIC`" line with:
> - [A new read function isn't granted to `mcp_reader`] → Retrieval fails with a permission error once a policy or view starts calling it. The allowlist test and the API integration tests catch this. Add `mcp_reader` to the security model's checklist for new functions.

**4. `tasks.md`, task 1.2**
> - [ ] 1.2 Grant `mcp_reader` `EXECUTE` on an allowlist, starting from `anon`'s read-only functions: the functions that the policies and views retrieval reads call. Follow the rules in `packages/database/doc/security_model.md`. Verify:
>   - a test lists every function `mcp_reader` can execute, and matches it against the allowlist;
>   - none of the write functions or `SECURITY DEFINER` write paths is executable by `mcp_reader`.

This drops the hosted-database check and the full-suite run as `anon` and `authenticated`, because those only guarded the revoke, and the revoke is already done.

**Not changed:** the proposal's "an `EXECUTE` allowlist" line is still accurate. Edit 3 adds a security model checklist item, but that file belongs to Marc-Antoine. I'd raise it with him in the Roam thread rather than edit it from this change.

content.text:
Partly. You're right that the search RPC is the only new database function. The retrieval "functions" in group 2 are TypeScript in `packages/database/src`, like `getSharedNodeByRid` (`sharedNodes.ts`). They read the `my_spaces`, `my_concepts` and `my_contents` views and call no RPC.

We still have to grant `mcp_reader` some existing functions, though. It's a new role, so it starts with `EXECUTE` on nothing: no function is executable through `PUBLIC` anymore, and the default privileges cover only `authenticated` and `service_role`. Postgres checks a function called inside a view or policy against the role running the query, not the view's owner (rule 2 in Marc-Antoine's doc). So when `mcp_reader` reads `my_concepts`, it needs `EXECUTE` on the helpers that view calls, such as `my_space_ids`, `my_user_accounts` and `my_accessible_resources`. Otherwise the read fails with a permission error instead of returning fewer rows.

So the allowlist covers two things:
1. **New:** the search RPC.
2. **Existing:** the access helpers the views and policies call, plus any functions we select through. `anon`'s read-only set already covers these, because public access reads the same views. We grant them; we don't write them.

There's also a shortcut to weigh, `GRANT anon TO mcp_reader`. The role would then inherit `anon`'s set, and future public-access grants would reach it automatically, so no separate list would drift. The catch is that `mcp_reader` would also inherit `get_secret_token`, which redeems a single-use token. That isn't a read, so I'd keep the explicit allowlist, matched against `anon`'s list in the test. I haven't changed the draft for any of this. It already says "starting from `anon`'s read-only functions", which fits.

-- **Row-level security.** 61 of the 65 row-level security policies have no `TO` clause, so they apply to every database role. +- **Row-level security.** 58 of the 62 row-level security policies have no `TO` clause, so they apply to every database role. The other four are `TO authenticated` on `storage.objects` (file storage), which retrieval doesn't read. Table grants go to `authenticated` (the signed-in role) and `service_role`. `anon` holds `SELECT` on `Space`, the contributor tables and the `my_*` views, ahead of public access ([ENG-1837](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1837)).

+- **Function privileges.** Every function is granted explicitly. `authenticated` gets every new function by default, and `anon` gets only a listed set of read-only functions. `packages/database/doc/security_model.md` gives the rules and the heuristic for granting new functions. Some write functions are `SECURITY DEFINER` (they run as their owner, not as the caller), such as `create_secret_token` and `accept_group_invitation`. Each is granted to `authenticated` only.
- **Auth settings.** `config.toml` sets `jwt_expiry = 3600` (a session token lasts one hour). The custom access token hook is commented out.
## Goals / Non-Goals

input.old_string:
**Locking down functions.** `PUBLIC` (every database role) holds `EXECUTE` on every function, so the allowlist needs two changes:

- `REVOKE EXECUTE ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC`;
- the matching default-privilege change, so new functions aren't executable by default either.

**This doesn't change what plugins or sync can do.** `base.sql` runs first and sets default privileges that grant every later function to `anon` and `authenticated` explicitly. So the plugins' roles don't rely on `PUBLIC`, and they keep every function they can call today. Postgres has no deny grant, and every role inherits `PUBLIC`, so removing that default is the only way to keep a function from `mcp_reader`. Before the revoke, a check on the hosted database confirms that `anon` and `authenticated` hold `EXECUTE` on every function. Its migrations predate the schema files, so it could differ.
input.new_string: **Granting functions.** The default privileges don't cover a new role, so `mcp_reader` starts with no `EXECUTE`. It gets an explicit allowlist: the search RPC, plus the existing helpers that the views and policies it reads call, such as `my_space_ids` and `my_accessible_resources`. The allowlist starts from `anon`'s read-only set, which public access already uses. Postgres checks a function called inside a view or policy against the querying role, so a missing grant fails the read with a permission error ([security model](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/blob/main/packages/database/doc/security_model.md), rules 1-2). A new read function that retrieval reaches needs a grant to `mcp_reader` too. Plugin and sync grants don't change.

input.string: **Row-level security.** 58 of the 62 row-level security policies have no `TO` clause, so they apply to every database role. The other four are `TO authenticated` on `storage.objects` (file storage), which retrieval doesn't read. input.string: **Function privileges.** Every function is granted explicitly. `authenticated` gets every new function by default, and `anon` gets only a listed set of read-only functions. `packages/database/doc/security_model.md` gives the rules and the heuristic for granting new functions. input.string: **Granting functions.** The default privileges don't cover a new role, so `mcp_reader` starts with no `EXECUTE`. It gets an explicit allowlist: the search RPC, plus the existing helpers that the views and policies it reads call, such as `my_space_ids` and `my_accessible_resources`. The allowlist starts from `anon`'s read-only set, which public access already uses. Postgres checks a function called inside a view or policy against the querying role, so a missing grant fails the read with a permission error ([security model](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/blob/main/packages/database/doc/security_model.md), rules 1-2). A new read function that retrieval reaches needs a grant to `mcp_reader` too. Plugin and sync grants don't change.
